title: Union-find, tries and prefix matching in Python
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Union-find with a parent list, nested-dict tries, wildcard search and IPv4 longest prefix match with shifts, plus recursion and dict pitfalls.
source: Python docs (ipaddress, bisect, dict, sys.setrecursionlimit); CLRS ch. 19-21; LeetCode Redundant Connection, Implement Trie, Design Add and Search Words; RFC 4632 (CIDR)

questions.prompt: Write a Python function count_components(n, edges) for an undirected graph with nodes 0..n-1, using union-find (a parent list and a find function with path compression or halving). Return the number of connected components.
questions.explanation: Counting successful unions and subtracting from n is the trick. Counting distinct roots at the end, or a DFS over adjacency lists, are valid alternatives (the DFS would not satisfy these union-find checks). The loop-based find avoids recursion limits. Time O((n + E) * alpha(n)).

checks.label: decrements the component count only when two roots differ

questions.prompt: Write a Python class Trie using nested dicts (dict of dicts), with insert(word) and search(word). search returns True only if the whole word was inserted, not merely a prefix of one.
questions.explanation: The end-of-word marker separates search("car") from startsWith("ca"). A TrieNode class with a children dict and is_end flag is equivalent. Insert and search are O(L).

checks.label: walks or creates a child per character
marks the end of a word with a sentinel key or flag
search checks the end marker, not just that the path exists

questions.prompt: A binary trie is made of dicts: node[0] and node[1] hold child nodes (when present) and node["hop"] holds the next hop if a route ends there. Write lookup(root, ip) that returns the next hop of the longest matching prefix (or None) for a 32-bit address held in a non-negative int, reading bits from the most significant one.
questions.explanation: Keep walking after the first match and remember the deepest hop. Python ints are unbounded and non-negative here, so >> needs no unsigned variant. With /0, /8, /16 and /24 routes, 10.1.3.7 returns the /16 hop.

checks.label: extracts bits with a shift and & 1
moves to the child for each bit
remembers the last route seen on the way down

questions.prompt: Write a Python class WordDictionary with add_word(word) and search(word), where search treats "." as any single letter. Use nested dicts and recursion.
questions.explanation: Without wildcards search is O(L); with k dots the worst case branches over the alphabet at each dot, up to O(26^k * L). The "$" end marker keeps words from matching as prefixes. LeetCode 211 (Design Add and Search Words).

checks.label: tries every child for a wildcard

questions.prompt: The IPv4 address 10.1.3.7 is held in a Python int as 0x0A010307. What does the expression (ip >> 8) & 0xFF evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Shifting right by 8 drops the last octet (7); masking with 0xFF keeps the next 8 bits, which are the third octet, 3. Python ints never wrap, so there is no sign issue for a non-negative address.
A /22 leaves 32 - 22 = 10 host bits, and 2^10 = 1024 addresses. num_addresses counts every address in the block, including the network and broadcast ones.

questions.prompt: In a trie of nested dicts, why is the end-of-word marker stored under a key such as "$" that cannot be a letter?
questions.explanation: Alternatives are a TrieNode class with an is_end flag or a separate set of full words. The marker is what makes search("ca") false when only "car" was inserted.

options.text: So the marker cannot collide with any child edge.
options.why: Correct: the special key separates edges from the terminal flag.

options.text: So the dict stays sorted and iteration returns words in alphabetical order.
options.why: Dict order is insertion order; the marker does not sort anything.

options.text: Because dict keys must be unique across the whole trie, not only per node.
options.why: Keys only need to be unique inside their own dict, so this is not the reason.

options.text: To make lookups O(1) regardless of the length of the word.
options.why: Walking the word still takes one dict lookup per character, O(L).

questions.prompt: A recursive find on a parent chain of 100,000 nodes fails with RecursionError under default settings. What is the most robust fix?
questions.explanation: Union by rank would also keep the chain short. In contests people raise the limit, but an iterative find is the portable answer.

options.text: Raise the recursion limit to 10**7 and keep the recursive version.
options.why: Deep recursion can still crash the interpreter with a stack overflow in the C stack.

options.text: Write find iteratively with path halving, so no call stack grows.
options.why: Correct: a loop uses constant stack, whatever the chain length.

options.text: Wrap the call in try/except RecursionError and retry once.
options.why: The retry hits the same limit, so the error just repeats.

options.text: Switch the parent list to a dict, which has a deeper stack.
options.why: The container type has no effect on call-stack depth.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit IPv4 address is stored as a non-negative Python int, for example 3232235521 for 192.168.0.1.
questions.explanation: Negative ints would be treated as infinite two's complement, so mask first: (ip & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> 31.
questions.assertion: (ip >> 31) & 1 extracts the top bit of the address.
questions.reason: Python ints have no fixed width, so a non-negative value is never sign-extended by >>.

whys.a: Right: for a non-negative int >> simply drops low bits, so the top bit is exactly bit 31; R is the reason it is safe.
whys.b: R is the reason, not an unrelated fact.

questions.prompt: A union-find built from a Python list.
questions.explanation: The default recursion limit is about 1000 frames, far below 100,000.
questions.assertion: A recursive find on a 100,000-node chain can raise RecursionError.
questions.reason: Python lists are dynamic arrays with amortised O(1) append.

whys.a: List append cost has nothing to do with the call stack depth.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but the list implementation does not explain the recursion error; the default recursion limit does.

questions.explanation: For huge vocabularies use arrays, compressed (radix) tries, or __slots__ node classes to cut the overhead.
questions.assertion: Every node of a nested-dict trie is a separate dict object.
questions.reason: An empty dict takes no memory in Python.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but even an empty dict occupies tens of bytes, so R is false and dict tries are memory hungry.

questions.prompt: A wildcard search loops over node.items() while a helper adds new keys to node.
questions.explanation: A search should not mutate the trie at all; do not use setdefault inside search, because it creates nodes.
questions.assertion: Adding keys to a dict while looping over it is safe.
questions.reason: Python raises RuntimeError when a dict changes size during iteration.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: R is true and is exactly why A is false; loop over list(node.items()) if you must modify.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement with the Python tool that fits best.
questions.explanation: dict gives O(1) exact lookup; bisect on a sorted list gives floor/ceiling in O(log n) (inserts are O(n)); nested dicts suit sparse alphabets; a list of parent ids is the union-find workhorse; Counter counts hashables. heapq is a priority queue, not a lookup structure.

left.text: Exact key lookup, no ordering needed
Sorted keys with floor and ceiling queries
Children of a trie node over any alphabet
Connectivity of node ids 0..n-1 under merges

right.text: A dict from character to child dict
